problem_data.story:
ZARA HOLMES
By BILL DOEDE

They lived in a modest apartment in Lincoln, Galdoria, near the central weather station. Once it had been employee housing for meteorologists during the great climate crisis. The government sold it after the crisis passed. Now Patricia Bell and her daughter were very comfortable, even during the unpredictable storm seasons. During the calmer months they consulted for independent weather forecasters, and Patricia had built a small media production studio in the spare bedroom. They were able to make ends meet.

Her neighbors knew nothing of the technology she had brought with her to Lincoln. They didn't even know that she was not a native. She never spoke of it, except at first, when Zara was a girl of seven and they had just come there to live. Then she only said that she came from the Foxwood Region. She knew the names of small towns there, and minor facts about them; it lent an air of authenticity to her claim of being a native. Actually her previous residence was Waverly, Ilvaria, where the Regulators had killed her husband.

That was back in '07, on the eve of his departure for the Mars colonies; but she never spoke of this; and she was very careful not to move from place to place except by the conventional methods of travel.

Also, she wore her hair long, almost to the shoulders. People said, "There goes one of the old-fashioned ones. That hair-do was popular back in the sixties." They did not suspect that she did this only to cover the thin, pencil-line scar, evidence that a small device lay under her skin behind the ear.

For Patricia Bell was one of the Transients.

Her husband had been one of the small group who developed this tiny instrument. Not the inventor—his name was Rafael Mason, and the effects produced by it were known as the Mason Effect. In appearance it resembled a small neural interface chip. Analysis by the best scientific minds proved it to be a quantum processor.

Yet it held the power to move a body instantly from one point in space to any other point. Each unit was custom built, keyed to operate only by the thought pattern of the particular individual and their emotional state—specifically, their capacity for empathy and cooperation.

Several times in the past seven years Patricia Bell had seen other Transients, and had been tempted to identify herself and say, "Here I am. You are one of them; so am I. Come, and we'll talk. We'll talk about Mason and Diego Wolfe, who helped them all get away. And Doctor Tomás Roberts. And my husband, who never got away because those filthy, unspeakable Regulators shot him in the back, there in that café in Waverly, Ilvaria."

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a man named Viktor Marsh came and stayed in the apartment below theirs.

She learned certain things about him gradually. He kept irregular hours, sometimes leaving before dawn and returning well past midnight. His curtains were always drawn. Once, she glimpsed documents spread across his table through a gap in the blinds—photographs, what looked like dossiers, names she couldn't read from that distance.

Patricia watched him for weeks. She noted how he studied the other residents, how his gaze lingered on people's ears and hairlines. She saw him speaking quietly into communication devices, using terminology she recognized from her years of hiding: "patterns," "traces," "confirmed sightings."

One morning, while returning borrowed tools, his identification fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands. The badge confirmed what she had suspected. All the loneliness returned in a black wave. She thought of her husband's body crumpling in that café, the news reaching her hours later, the way everything she loved had been taken from her by people who carried badges just like this one.

That night she soundlessly lifted the window over his bed and shot him with a silenced pistol.

She threw the weapon into the river. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators all over Earth; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Zara, was grown.

Together they would seek revenge. She did not have the device for Zara—not yet. But she would. The Transients took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned the small patch of gauze would be behind her ear. She would shield her until the opening healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek revenge.

Later they would go to Mars, where a life free from Regulators could be lived.

It happened to Zara one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Patricia Bell was working in her studio, editing weather forecasts for local media production; Zara supposedly was at the community pool with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her, dripping wet in her swimsuit. At sight of her mother her face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Patricia was forced to hold her to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the pool, where her friends were still swimming with great noise and delight. Apparently they did not miss her. Patricia Bell handed her a towel. "Here, dry yourself off. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Patricia stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well get used to it now."

"Get used to what?"

"To people seeing you unprepared."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was swimming in the pool, and a woman came down to the pool. Her hair was silver-white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Zara Holmes, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a vehicle and there was another woman in it, that looked like the first one only she was taller. We went to a building, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a table, sort of. A high table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some language I don't know."

Zara ran her hand through her wet hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be here with you. And then I was here."

Zara faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better dry off," Patricia Bell said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful."

"But what happened? What is this patch behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped in the act of drying herself. "Guess I know now. They made me a Transient."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Patricia called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too." She paused, something shifting in her expression. "I remember something from when I was little. The man who lived downstairs—Viktor, I think his name was. He disappeared one night."

Patricia's hands stilled on the towel she was folding.

"I wasn't sleeping that night," Zara continued slowly. "I was afraid to stay inside alone, so I followed you. I saw you go to his window. I saw you..." She trailed off, studying her mother's face.

Patricia felt the color drain from her cheeks. "You were only nine."

"I never told anyone. They would have taken you away."

For a long moment, neither spoke. Then Zara asked quietly, "Why did you do it, Mother? Was it because of what he was?"

Patricia Bell held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So she sat across the kitchen table from her, and Patricia told the whole history, beginning with Rafael Mason sitting in the laboratory in the Larchmont Region, holding in his hand a small device crafted from quantum-entangled particles with controlled consciousness states. He had made it, looking for a better way to study consciousness studies and neural interfaces. He was holding this device... and it was a cold day outside... and he was dreaming of a warm beach on Mars—

And suddenly he was there, on the beach. He could not believe it at first. He felt the sand and thin atmosphere, and felt of himself; there was no mistake.

On the shuttle back to Earth he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more devices. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it, and he kept the secret, giving devices to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it a quantum entanglement of cooperative consciousness, which was very undefinitive.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until one night a Regulator arrested one man for corporate espionage. It was a valid charge. One disadvantage of this method of travel was that, while a body could travel instantaneously to any chosen spot, it sometimes arrived without all belongings intact.

The arrested man disappeared from his cell, and the next morning the Regulator was found dead in his office. This set off a campaign against Transients. One base act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as human.

Patricia told how Rafael Mason, knowing he had made too many devices and given them unwisely, left Earth for Mars.

He went alone, not knowing if he could go so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in an abandoned weather station in the Foxwood Region—and disappeared in a body, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at the sky.

"You asked about Viktor Marsh," Patricia said, her voice hardening. "He was one of them—a Regulator. They hunt us, Zara. They've been hunting us since the beginning."

"But why did you—"

"Your father was one of the great ones," Patricia continued, her eyes distant, "along with Mason and Diego Wolfe and Dr. Tomás Roberts. He helped plan the escape to Mars. But the Regulators found him in Waverly fifteen minutes before the group left. They shot him in the back, and the others had to go on without him."

She paused, her hands gripping the edge of the table. "Your father was a great man, and I loved him. Every time I see one of their badges, I remember how they took him from us."

"I don't blame you, mother," Zara said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says, 'Transient' as if it is something dirty. They write it on the walls in public spaces."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them?"

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Patricia Bell watched Zara leave the apartment, walking slowly along the river, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the pool area, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would cross the river and enter the park there. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not travel far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within walking distance of familiar places, because she still lacked the tricks others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Patricia Bell changed into light clothes and went down to the river to cool herself in the breeze.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, taking longer and longer jumps, until Zara's confidence allowed her to reach any part of Earth she chose. Patricia knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a spot sufficiently remote to insure detection, Patricia would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly return to Lincoln. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only traces of a woman and a girl. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Patricia Bell as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Mason took his group to Mars, that individuals had thought patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their detectors, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Patricia Bell had gone to Mars with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Mason had selected only the best of the Transients when he left Earth, leaving all those with sociopathic tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more lucrative to stay. On Earth they could steal, manipulate corporate governance, even murder—without fear of the law.

Zara changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Zara," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs about sustainable business and economic development, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Patricia would repeat all the things she remembered about Mason and Diego Wolfe and Tomás Roberts. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Diego's partner, Mila Owen, and try to describe the horror in Mila's young mind when the news went out that Zara's father had been killed. She wanted her to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after Zara. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of hate.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Patricia Bell wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Hate, hate! Hate! You must learn to hate!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that she would learn it faster if she avoided the word.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Zara was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Zara referred to the "damn Regulators" now with a curl of her lip. They had been successful in contacting other Transients, and sometimes visited them at a remote rendezvous.

"When you have finished university," Patricia Bell told her daughter, "we will go to Mars."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the organizational development of the colony. Mason is a physicist, Diego Wolfe a systems engineer, Tomás Roberts a doctor. But Roberts is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Zara. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Focus on public health and mentorship—those will be valued skills."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Zara would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she retrieved the money she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Lincoln was sold. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Patricia Bell furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Zara's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of medical students.

It was also convenient for coming home late at night after Regulator hunting.

Patricia Bell was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Zara facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were evil creatures, tools of a decadent, bloodthirsty system, living off the fat of the land while suppressing technological progress and labor relations reforms.

She painted the room herself, in soft, neutral colors. When it was finished she showed Zara proudly into the room, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study sessions students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," she answered, "not here. No Transients will be at the university."

"Why not? Mason selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the device is taken and adjusted to a new thought pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Transients will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Patricia said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable."

She shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

Patricia said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being alone, at your age. Most young people do."

"I'm not like most young people, mother. The Transients saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Jessica Valdez?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how her hair fell over her face when she read, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Jess—' just as if I was human—'can I take you to the concert?'"

Patricia Bell turned to leave the room, but Zara stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Transient. You always will be a Transient. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and slammed the door. Zara stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been happy for her. Patricia was crying just beyond the wall.

Zara did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the device was out of the question for them now, anyway.

In the spring Patricia Bell caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Zara moved into the new bedroom. At first Patricia thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day she disappeared.

Patricia Bell was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Transients being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Transient had raided the Regulator's office in a distant city, killing three, and getting killed himself. Patricia Bell immediately traveled there conventionally. She did not consider the risk. In the city she found clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain man had been a rogue Transient, one of those left behind by Mason as unsuitable. His partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. He had gone completely insane and made the raid singlehanded. Patricia Bell read the account of crimes committed by the man and his partner, and determined to prevent Zara from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she arrived at her own home, Zara was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that fight."

She shook her head.

Patricia stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a sheet of paper. She was proud of her daughter's profile, dark-haired and strong, handsome in a striking way. She cracked her knuckles nervously.

"What did you do?" Patricia asked.

Suddenly she flung the pen down, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Waverly."

Patricia Bell had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to get at the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the people who killed Father." She said the word strangely. She was unaccustomed to it.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the paper on her desk. Patricia Bell, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches on paper, evil sounds, like whispers of betrayal. "Priya Torres" didn't sound evil; neither did "Marcus Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Zara to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for revenge. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask why I broke in without breaking the lock or even a window. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your damn business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Transients must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Transients? We hunt them because there is no prison in the world that will hold a Transient. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us.'"

Patricia Bell was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Patricia Bell stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Patricia Bell gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. She had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to the painted walls. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the people were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over Earth. In the killing of Transients, some devices might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the devices gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to gain them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the people on Zara's list might have acquired a device and were now Transients themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Priya Torres had been killed by a Transient. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Zara's desk.

She took the news feed into Zara's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. Her name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Transient is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Waverly will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Zara asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

She removed her hand from her arm. Her nails were digging into her flesh. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me. I can't hate them the way you do."

Patricia Bell's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped her face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Patricia breathing hard from the exertion, Zara stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that she could hate so suddenly, viciously.

She controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, testing them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive their vehicles through every city on Earth with those new detectors, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Zara sat down suddenly, "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no person can live this way."

She did not answer her. Finally Zara said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's coming. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was here. Zara saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely silver. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to relax. She was dressed simply in neutral clothing... and it seemed natural and right.

Then Patricia Bell saw her.

"Diego!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was afraid of so many things, but he was brave when it mattered."

Zara said, "Why was my father killed?"

"By mistake. Back in those days, like now, there were good Transients and bad. One of those not selected by Mason to join us was enraged, half crazy with envy. He killed two officials there in Waverly. The Regulators thought your father did it. Your father was the greatest person among us. It was he who first conceived the theory that there was a basic, underlying principle in the operation of the devices. Even now, no one knows how the idea of cooperation and empathy ties in with the Mason Effect; but we do know that hate and selfishness as motivating forces can greatly minimize the devices' power. That is why the undesirables with devices have never reached Mars."

Heavy steps sounded on the porch outside.

"We'd better hurry," Patricia Bell said.

Diego Wolfe held out her hands. They took them, to increase the power of the devices. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Patricia Bell flicked one thought of hatred at them, but of course they did not hear her. Diego's hands gripped tightly.

Patricia Bell slowly opened her eyes....

She no longer felt the hands. She was still in the room! Diego and her daughter were gone. Her power was gone!

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. She stared at them, then ran to Zara's desk, fumbling for the weapon.

The Regulators' weapons rattled.

Empathy, Diego said, the greatest of these is empathy and cooperation. Or did someone else say that? Someone, somewhere, perhaps in another time, in some misty, forgotten moment long gone, in another frame of reference perhaps....

Patricia Bell could not remember, before she died.
